results.title: Solving Reproducibility Challenges in Deep Learning and LLMs: Our Journey
results.content: Most ZKP use cases require a public verifier, meaning any CUDA-enabled device must be able to reproduce the AI computation, without enforcing a specific hardware architecture. In this blog post we detail our journey toward ensuring that our deep learning models consistently produce reproducible results. By controlling the order in which operations are performed, we can ensure that the computations are consistent across runs and hardware. We investigated the issue across multiple frameworks, starting with PyTorch, a leading platform for deep learning development, and continuing with llama.cpp, which is gaining traction as a popular framework for LLM inference, particularly for quantized models. Our first approach was to employ reproducibility flags provided by deep learning frameworks like PyTorch and control random number generators. import random import numpy as np import torch random.seed(0) # Sets the seed for Python's built-in random module (0) # Sets the seed for NumPy's random number generator torch.manual_seed(0) # Sets the seed for PyTorch's CPU random number generator torch.cuda.manual_seed(0) # Sets the seed for the current GPU device torch.cuda.manual_seed_all(0) # Sets the seed for all available GPU devices torch.use_deterministic_algorithms(True) # Ensures that only deterministic algorithms are used .matmul.allow_tf32 = False # Disables TensorFloat32 (TF32) on matmul ops .allow_tf32 = False # Disables TF32 on cuDNN .benchmark = False # Disables the cuDNN auto-tuner .deterministic = True # Forces cuDNN to use deterministic algorithms #in the worst case, use this: .enabled = False # Disables cuDNN entirely. Despite setting all possible seeds and disabling non-deterministic behaviors, the inherent non-associativity of floating-point operations, combined with hardware differences, continued to cause inconsistencies. As a result, despite storing weights in a quantized format, the model still relies on floating-point computations at runtime, which are subject to non-associativity and hardware variability. However, this high level of optimization sometimes comes at the cost of reproducibility, leading to different results across various hardware. By restricting computations to CUDA cores, we ensured that operations were executed in a consistent manner across different architectures, as different architectures might have different generations of Tensor cores. * **Hardware Matters:** Differences in GPU architectures can affect reproducibility, even when running the same code.

results.title: Reproducibility with GPUs. While trying to replicate and compare… | by Sakshi Bhatia | Medium
results.content: # Reproducibility with GPUs. While trying to replicate and compare experiments, you probably set the seed as follows for reproducibility:. seed = #torch.manual_seed(seed)(seed)random.seed(seed). But these are not the only sources of randomness when you’re running your experiments on a GPU. In this story, we assume that you are running experiments with PyTorch and CUDA and will cover the various sources of randomness and how we can fix those. 1. For operations that make use of torch.cuda random number generator, or if you’re doing multi-GPU training, CUDA might use a different seed for different operations/GPUs. For consistency, set *\_seed\_all(seed)*. 2. CUDA’s Deep Neural Network Library, CuDNN provides optimized GPU implementations for deep learning operations like Pooling, convolutions, normalization, etc. PyTorch calls this library for various processes, under the hood. Some CuDNN operations can have multiple valid implementations, and some of these implementations can be non-deterministic in nature. To ensure that the algorithms are implemented deterministically, set *.deterministic = True.*. 3. Additionally, CuDNN benchmarks different algorithms to pick the fastest one for your hardware. This is another source of non-determinism. Even on the same machine, the benchmark may select different algorithms due to benchmarking noise. To avoid that, set *.benchmark = False.*. 4. Note that points 2 and 3 pick the deterministic implementation, which may not always be the most optimal one, and hence might affect your training speed. Also, some PyTorch operations might not have a deterministic implementation at all; in that case, you would see an error like this. 5. Randomness may also creep in if you’re loading data using multiple workers. Use the following code snippet to fix this:. def seed_worker(worker_id): worker_seed = torch.initial_seed() % 2**32 (worker_seed) random.seed(worker_seed)g = torch.Generator()g.manual_seed(0)DataLoader( train_dataset, batch_size=batch_size, num_workers=num_workers, worker_init_fn=seed_worker, generator=g,). 6. Some other sources of possible randomness are:. a. GPU kernels don’t always execute in the same order due to CUDA’s parallel scheduling. This can cause tiny floating-point differences that grow over training runs. b. External libraries: Some augmentations or data loading may call into libraries outside PyTorch, example OpenCV, PIL, etc. If a seed is not set for these separately, randomness may creep in. ## Written by Sakshi Bhatia. ## No responses yet.

results.content: You can see from the example above that Numpy's RNG behaves the same way as Python's RNG: once a seed is set, the generator outputs the very same sequence of numbers, 6, 3, 7, and 4. But, it turns out, even though Numpy's legacy code and Python's random module use the same algorithm, and we're using the same seed in both of them, the generated numbers are *still* different! PyTorch can actually take care of itself in the above situation — it seeds each worker with a different number, that is, `base_seed + worker_id`, but it cannot take care of other packages (e.g. Numpy or Python's random module). Now every worker will use a different seed for PyTorch, Numpy, and Python's random module. Maybe you don't, but it's better to **play safe and set seeds for everything: PyTorch, Numpy, and even Python's random module**, and that's what we did in the previous section.
